name: OMK 2A Psych Exam 2 — Batch 5: Personality Disorders, Eating Disorders, Somatoform, Dissociative & Sexual

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the office by her roommate, who is worried about her eating. Over the past 8 months she has restricted her intake to roughly 600 calories daily and runs 10 miles most days. In the past 3 months she has additionally had about two episodes weekly in which she eats an entire container of ice cream and a box of cereal within an hour, feeling unable to stop, and afterward induces vomiting. She states that her goal is to keep losing weight and that she still looks 'heavy' in the mirror. Height is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) and weight is 44.5 kg (98 lb); BMI is 15.8 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.1°C (97.0°F), pulse is 46/min, and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. Examination shows fine downy hair over the forearms and cool extremities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: F. Other specified feeding or eating disorder
questions.explanation: Work the algorithm in order: check the BMI first, then identify the driving behavior. At 15.8 kg/m2 she is well below normal, which points hard at anorexia, and anorexia must be excluded before bulimia can be diagnosed. All three anorexia criteria are met — restriction of intake, fear of weight gain with no comfort reached at a lower weight, and body image distortion ('I still look heavy'). Her binge-purge episodes over the past 3 months set the subtype, not the diagnosis. Board pearl — the driving factor separates these disorders: anorexia restricts to keep losing weight, bulimia binges then compensates to avoid gaining, and binge eating disorder binges with no compensation at all. She is still chasing further weight loss.  [Learning objectives: LO 008, 038, 067]

wrongExplanations.0: The restricting subtype requires that no recurrent binge-eating or purging behavior has occurred in the past 3 months. She has had roughly two binge-purge episodes weekly during exactly that window, which assigns the other subtype.
wrongExplanations.1: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder involves restriction driven by lack of interest in food, sensory aversion, or fear of aversive consequences such as choking — explicitly without fear of weight gain or body image disturbance. She has both.
wrongExplanations.3: Binge eating disorder requires binges with no compensatory behavior, and is typically associated with a normal or elevated BMI. She purges after every binge and her BMI is 15.8 kg/m2.
wrongExplanations.4: This is the trap for a reader who anchors on the binge-purge cycle. Bulimia nervosa can only be diagnosed once anorexia is excluded, and it characteristically occurs at a normal-to-elevated BMI. Her BMI of 15.8 kg/m2 and her stated goal of continued weight loss both point away from it.
wrongExplanations.5: This residual category is for presentations where the pattern is clear but a threshold is not met — such as an anorexia pattern at a BMI of 19. She meets full anorexia criteria, so a residual category is unnecessary.

questions.eli5: She is very underweight, still thinks she looks heavy, and is trying to lose more. She does binge and throw up sometimes, but because losing weight is the goal and her weight is so low, this is anorexia — the bingeing just tells you which kind.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman meets full DSM-5 criteria for anorexia nervosa. Height is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) and weight is 38.6 kg (85 lb); BMI is 14.2 kg/m2. Which of the following severity specifiers best applies?
questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa severity is graded entirely by BMI: mild is 18.5 to 17, moderate is 16.99 to 16, severe is 15.99 to 15, and extreme is below 15. At 14.2 kg/m2 she falls below the 15 cutoff, making this the extreme specifier. Board pearl — the parallel structure is worth holding side by side: anorexia's severity is defined by BMI, while bulimia's is defined by the number of compensatory behaviors per week (mild 1 to 3, moderate 4 to 7, severe 8 to 13, extreme 14 or more).  [Learning objectives: LO 008]

wrongExplanations.0: Mild corresponds to a BMI of 18.5 to 17, the band just below the normal-weight threshold. She is more than 3 points below that range.
wrongExplanations.1: Moderate corresponds to a BMI of 16.99 to 16, which she is well below.
wrongExplanations.2: Severe corresponds to a BMI of 15.99 to 15. At 14.2 kg/m2 she has crossed beneath that floor into the next band.
wrongExplanations.4: Unspecified is not a severity specifier for anorexia. The unspecified label is a separate diagnostic category used when a clear eating-disorder pattern does not meet a required threshold, such as an anorexia pattern at a BMI of 19.

questions.eli5: Doctors grade how severe anorexia is using BMI alone. Anything under 15 is the most severe category, called extreme, and hers is 14.2.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a 2-year history of bulimia nervosa comes to the office for follow-up. She acknowledges binge eating four to five times weekly followed by compensatory behavior, but declines to say which method she uses. Height is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) and weight is 57 kg (126 lb); BMI is 21.5 kg/m2. Pulse is 96/min and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg, dropping to 88/58 mm Hg on standing. Examination shows normal dentition, no parotid enlargement, and no calluses or abrasions over the dorsum of either hand. Serum studies show sodium 131 mEq/L, potassium 3.0 mEq/L, chloride 112 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 16 mEq/L. Which of the following compensatory behaviors do these findings most support?
questions.explanation: Purging method can be read off the acid-base panel. Laxative abuse causes loss of bicarbonate-rich stool, producing a metabolic ACIDOSIS with low sodium and HIGH chloride — exactly her pattern of bicarbonate 16 mEq/L with chloride 112 mEq/L. Self-induced vomiting does the opposite, losing gastric acid to produce a metabolic ALKALOSIS with LOW chloride and low potassium. The negative examination is doing real work here: absent dental erosion, absent parotid enlargement, and absent Russell sign all argue against vomiting. Board pearl — vomiting gives alkalosis with low chloride and low potassium; laxatives give acidosis with low sodium and high chloride. Hypokalemia is common to both.  [Learning objectives: LO 008, 067]

wrongExplanations.1: Vomiting produces a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis — a high bicarbonate with a low chloride, the mirror image of her panel. The absence of dental erosion, parotid enlargement, and knuckle calluses (Russell sign) independently argues against it.
wrongExplanations.2: Diuretic misuse typically produces a contraction alkalosis with hypokalemia, again raising rather than lowering the bicarbonate, and would not generate a hyperchloremic acidosis.
wrongExplanations.3: Excessive exercise is a non-purging compensatory behavior and does not by itself produce this electrolyte and acid-base derangement.
wrongExplanations.4: Fasting between binges is likewise a non-purging behavior and would not generate a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia.
wrongExplanations.5: Ipecac induces vomiting, so it would produce the alkalotic pattern rather than this acidosis. It is also historically noted for cardiomyopathy, and its sale is now restricted so it is rarely encountered.

questions.eli5: She would not say how she purges, but her blood chemistry tells on her. Throwing up leaves the blood too basic; laxatives leave it too acidic, and hers is acidic.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the office because of distress over her eating. For the past 14 months she has eaten unusually large quantities of food within 2 hours, at least four times weekly, with a sense that she cannot stop; she eats past the point of feeling full, eats alone because she is embarrassed, and feels guilty afterward. She has never induced vomiting, used laxatives or diuretics, fasted, or exercised to compensate. She has completed 6 months of cognitive behavioral therapy with only modest improvement and wishes to add medication. Height is 165 cm (5 ft 5 in) and weight is 90 kg (198 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m2. Pulse is 72/min and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. She has no cardiovascular disease, no history of substance use disorder, and no seizure history; electrocardiography shows normal sinus rhythm with a QTc of 424 ms. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
questions.explanation: Binges with a sense of loss of control, eating past fullness, eating alone from embarrassment, and guilt — with NO compensatory behavior at all — defines binge eating disorder. Lisdexamfetamine is the agent FDA-approved for moderate-to-severe binge eating disorder and reduces binge frequency. The stem deliberately clears every objection to a stimulant: no cardiovascular disease, normal blood pressure and pulse, no substance use history, and a normal QTc. Board pearl — best outcomes in binge eating disorder come from medication PLUS therapy rather than either alone, which is why adding a drug after a partial CBT response is the right move rather than switching strategies.  [Learning objectives: LO 023, 077]

wrongExplanations.0: Fluoxetine is the SSRI with an FDA indication for bulimia nervosa, not binge eating disorder. Bulimia requires recurrent compensatory behavior, which she explicitly has never had.
wrongExplanations.2: Ondansetron is an antiemetic used to reduce purging behavior in bulimia. She does not purge, so there is nothing for it to target.
wrongExplanations.3: Topiramate does reduce binge frequency and appetite and is a legitimate option in binge eating disorder, but lisdexamfetamine is the agent that carries the actual FDA approval for this indication.
wrongExplanations.4: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and carries a black-box warning in eating disorders; it is not an evidence-based treatment for binge eating disorder and is the agent to avoid rather than select in this population.

questions.eli5: She binges but never makes up for it afterward, which makes it binge eating disorder. Lisdexamfetamine is the one medicine officially approved for that, and her heart and blood pressure are healthy enough to take it safely.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents after fainting at school. She has restricted her intake for 14 months and states she needs to lose 'about ten more pounds.' Height is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) and weight is 40.8 kg (90 lb); BMI is 14.1 kg/m2. Temperature is 35.8°C (96.4°F), pulse is 42/min, and blood pressure is 84/52 mm Hg supine, falling to 68/40 mm Hg on standing with a pulse of 58/min. Serum studies show potassium 3.1 mEq/L, phosphate 2.1 mg/dL, and magnesium 1.4 mg/dL. Electrocardiography shows sinus bradycardia with a QTc of 468 ms. She denies suicidal ideation. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
choices: A. Outpatient fluoxetine with weekly weight checks
B. Outpatient olanzapine for appetite stimulation
C. Outpatient cognitive behavioral therapy alone
D. Rapid high-calorie refeeding to restore weight quickly
E. Inpatient medical stabilization with gradual refeeding
questions.explanation: Medical stabilization always precedes psychiatric treatment in anorexia nervosa. Her bradycardia at 42/min, profound orthostasis, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia, and prolonged QTc are not incidental findings — they are the reason anorexia carries the highest mortality of any psychiatric diagnosis. Weight restoration proceeds at roughly 1 pound per week under monitoring, because refeeding too aggressively drives an insulin surge that shifts phosphate, potassium, and magnesium intracellularly and precipitates refeeding syndrome, and her already-low phosphate and magnesium mark her as high risk. Board pearl — no medication is FDA-approved for anorexia nervosa, so any drug on this list is at best adjunctive and none of them addresses the acute danger.  [Learning objectives: LO 023, 067, 077]

wrongExplanations.0: SSRIs can stimulate appetite and treat comorbid depression or anxiety, but no medication is FDA-approved for anorexia, and outpatient management ignores a pulse of 42/min, a QTc of 468 ms, and three electrolyte derangements.
wrongExplanations.1: Olanzapine is used off-label for its appetite-stimulating effect in anorexia, but it prolongs the QT interval and would be started in a patient whose QTc is already 468 ms — and again, outpatient management is unsafe at these vitals.
wrongExplanations.2: CBT is the cornerstone of anorexia treatment, but it is what happens AFTER medical stabilization. Therapy cannot be delivered to a hemodynamically unstable patient, and delaying stabilization is the dangerous choice.
wrongExplanations.3: This is the trap for a reader who correctly identifies that she needs to gain weight. Rapid high-calorie refeeding is precisely what precipitates refeeding syndrome, and her low phosphate and magnesium already flag her as high risk for it.

questions.eli5: Her heart is beating dangerously slowly and her body salts are low, so she needs the hospital before she needs therapy or pills. Food has to be added back slowly, because feeding someone too fast after starvation can be deadly.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman restricts her intake to roughly 800 calories daily, exercises for 2 hours most days, expresses intense fear of gaining weight, and states that she sees herself as overweight despite objective evidence to the contrary. She has had no binge episodes and no purging behavior. Height is 168 cm (5 ft 6 in) and weight is 53.5 kg (118 lb); BMI is 19 kg/m2. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
choices: C. Other specified feeding or eating disorder
questions.explanation: The driving-factor pattern is unmistakably anorexic — restriction aimed at further weight loss, fear of gaining, and body image distortion — but the BMI does not clear the threshold, sitting at 19 kg/m2 within the normal range. When the pattern is clear but a required cutoff is not met, the correct label is the other specified or unspecified feeding and eating disorder category. Board pearl — this is a legitimate clinical category rather than a cop-out; the DSM draws sharp lines and real patients fall between them, and this exact scenario (an anorexia pattern at a BMI of 19) is the standard illustration.  [Learning objectives: LO 008, 038]

wrongExplanations.0: Anorexia nervosa requires significantly low body weight relative to what is minimally expected, and the severity specifiers themselves start at a BMI of 18.5. At 19 kg/m2 she does not meet the weight criterion.
wrongExplanations.1: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder requires that restriction NOT be driven by fear of weight gain or body image disturbance. She has both, which is the explicit exclusion for this diagnosis.
wrongExplanations.3: Binge eating disorder requires recurrent binge episodes with loss of control. She has had none.
wrongExplanations.4: Bulimia nervosa requires both recurrent binges and recurrent compensatory behavior at least weekly for 3 months. She has neither.

questions.eli5: She thinks and behaves exactly like someone with anorexia, but her weight has not dropped far enough to meet the official cutoff. There is a real category for that in-between situation.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman comes to the office at her sister's insistence. Her sister reports that on a single afternoon last week the patient went from 'ecstatic' after her boyfriend answered a text, to sobbing and threatening to hurt herself 40 minutes later when he did not answer a second one, to calm again by dinner. This pattern occurs several times most weeks and has for years. She has had six relationships in 3 years, each beginning with the partner described as 'perfect' and ending with them described as 'a monster.' She reports a chronic sense of emptiness and has superficial linear scars on both forearms. She sleeps 7 to 8 hours nightly, including during her most agitated periods, and has never had a stretch of days with reduced need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, or grandiosity. Urine toxicology screening is negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: E. Major depressive disorder with mixed features
questions.explanation: This diagnosis turns on timing, not symptom content. Borderline affective instability shifts within hours, is reactive to a specific interpersonal trigger (an unanswered text), and sits inside a broader pattern of unstable relationships, identity, and self-harm. Bipolar episodes last weeks to months, recur roughly every couple of years, and shift relatively autonomously of triggers. The buried clue is the sleep: decreased need for sleep is a core, reliable feature of mania and hypomania, and she sleeps 7 to 8 hours even at her most agitated. Board pearl — borderline is misdiagnosed as bipolar throughout patients' lifetimes, so ask two questions: how long does the episode last, and what set it off?  [Learning objectives: LO 041, 089]

wrongExplanations.1: Bipolar I requires at least one manic episode lasting 7 or more days, or any duration with hospitalization or psychosis. Her mood shifts resolve within an afternoon, and she has never had reduced sleep need, grandiosity, or increased goal-directed activity.
wrongExplanations.2: Bipolar II requires a hypomanic episode of at least 4 consecutive days plus a major depressive episode. Her shifts last under an hour and are triggered by specific relational events, which is the opposite of an autonomous sustained episode.
wrongExplanations.3: Cyclothymic disorder requires 2 years of numerous subsyndromal hypomanic and depressive periods. Hypomanic-level symptoms are entirely absent, and her instability is reactive rather than cyclic.
wrongExplanations.4: Mixed features require a major depressive episode with 3 or more manic or hypomanic symptoms most days. Neither the depressive episode nor the manic symptoms are present; the pattern is minutes-to-hours emotional reactivity.

questions.eli5: Her mood flips several times in one afternoon depending on whether her boyfriend texts back, and she still sleeps fine. Bipolar mood changes last weeks and come with not needing sleep, so this is the personality pattern instead.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder has had three emergency department visits in 6 months for superficial self-inflicted lacerations following arguments with her partner. She is currently taking no medications, denies active suicidal ideation, and is willing to engage in ongoing treatment. She has no psychotic symptoms, no substance use disorder, and no history of a manic or major depressive episode. Vital signs are within normal limits and laboratory studies are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Borderline personality disorder is the one personality disorder with a dedicated, disorder-specific first-line psychotherapy. Dialectical behavior therapy was created by Marsha Linehan for exactly this population and is built around four skills modules that map onto borderline's four dysregulation domains: core mindfulness for cognitive dysregulation, distress tolerance for impulsiveness, emotion regulation for labile affect, and interpersonal effectiveness for relational chaos. Board pearl — the exam shortcut is that DBT is technically a form of CBT, so if DBT appears as an option and the vignette is borderline, choose DBT; if it does not appear, choose CBT, which is the mainstay for the other nine personality disorders.  [Learning objectives: LO 002, 020, 089]

wrongExplanations.0: CBT is the correct default for the other nine personality disorders and would be the answer if DBT were not offered. When both appear and the vignette is specifically borderline, DBT is the more specific and correct choice.
wrongExplanations.1: Supportive psychotherapy — listening, encouragement, and stability — fits acute crises and acute medical comorbidity, such as consultation-liaison work. It is not a definitive treatment for a chronic personality disorder with recurrent self-harm.
wrongExplanations.2: Interpersonal psychotherapy is a structured, time-limited treatment focused on current relationships and communication, most often used in depression. It does not target the impulsivity and emotion dysregulation driving her self-harm.
wrongExplanations.4: Psychodynamic psychotherapy is exploratory and long-course. Some research does favor transference-focused therapy for impulsivity and anger in borderline patients, but DBT remains the standard first-line and most widely tested answer.

questions.eli5: Borderline personality disorder is the only one of the ten with its own custom-built therapy. DBT teaches four sets of skills that match exactly the four things this disorder makes hard.

questions.stem: A medication is prescribed to a patient with a personality disorder. This prescription is best characterized as which of the following?
choices: A. An FDA-approved treatment for the personality disorder itself
B. An off-label agent targeting specific symptom domains of the disorder
C. First-line monotherapy that can substitute for psychotherapy
D. An FDA-approved treatment for the impulsivity domain only
E. Contraindicated in all patients with a personality disorder
questions.explanation: There is no FDA-approved medication for any of the ten DSM-5 personality disorders — not one, for any of them. Every medication used is off-label and targets a symptom domain arising from the disorder: affective instability, impulsivity, transient psychosis, or self-destructive behavior. The APA recommends medication as adjunctive only, never as monotherapy for the disorder itself. Board pearl — despite that weak evidence base, polypharmacy is common in practice, with more than half of borderline patients on two psychotropics and more than 11% on five or more; quetiapine has the most notable single result, an 82% response versus 48% for placebo on the Zanarini Rating Scale, and it is still off-label.  [Learning objectives: LO 069, 089]

wrongExplanations.0: No personality disorder has an FDA-approved pharmacotherapy. This is the single most important pharmacologic fact about the group.
wrongExplanations.2: Psychotherapy is primary for every personality disorder — DBT for borderline, CBT for the other nine — and medication never substitutes for it.
wrongExplanations.3: There is no FDA approval for any domain of any personality disorder, including impulsivity. Domain-targeted prescribing happens, but it is off-label.
wrongExplanations.4: Medications are not contraindicated; they are routinely and appropriately used off-label for specific symptoms such as depression, irritability, or transient psychotic phenomena.

questions.eli5: No pill has ever been officially approved to treat any personality disorder. Doctors still use medicines, but only to take the edge off particular symptoms, not to fix the underlying pattern.

questions.stem: Desmond is a 34-year-old man who lives alone in the apartment where he grew up. Neighbors describe him as strange: he wears three mismatched layers of clothing in July and mutters greetings in phrasing they find hard to follow, once telling a neighbor that her mail 'arrived in the wrong direction.' He believes that by concentrating hard at intersections he can change traffic lights, and he has told his case manager that certain television broadcasts contain messages meant specifically for him. He becomes visibly anxious in groups and keeps his distance from others, whom he suspects of laughing at him behind his back, though he says he would like to have people to talk to. He has never had a hallucination, and his thought process, while circumstantial, remains followable. He has held the same part-time night stocking job for 9 years. This pattern has been present since his early twenties. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Schizotypal personality disorder is the only diagnosis that combines all four elements here: odd appearance and behavior, odd speech, magical thinking and ideas of reference (changing traffic lights by concentration, broadcasts meant for him), and social anxiety with suspiciousness — captured by the UFO AIDER mnemonic. It sits in Cluster A, the odd and eccentric group, which carries the strongest genetic link to schizophrenia. Board pearl — the discriminator against schizophrenia is that these are attenuated, not frank, psychotic phenomena: no hallucinations, followable thought process, and 9 years of stable employment argue for a lifelong personality pattern rather than a psychotic illness with functional decline.  [Learning objectives: LO 041, 069]

wrongExplanations.0: Avoidant personality disorder involves fear of criticism and rejection with a genuine desire for connection, but it does not include odd beliefs, magical thinking, ideas of reference, or eccentric speech and appearance. His magical thinking is what excludes it.
wrongExplanations.1: Borderline personality disorder centers on unstable relationships and identity, abandonment fears, impulsivity, and affective instability. None of that is described; he has held one job for 9 years and has no pattern of turbulent relationships.
wrongExplanations.2: Paranoid personality disorder involves pervasive distrust and assumption of malicious motive, which he partly shows — but it does not include the magical thinking, ideas of reference, odd speech, and eccentric appearance that dominate this picture.
wrongExplanations.3: Schizoid personality disorder involves genuine indifference to relationships and a real preference for solitude. He explicitly says he would like people to talk to, and schizoid does not include odd beliefs or ideas of reference.
wrongExplanations.4: Schizophrenia requires at least 6 months of disturbance with two or more active-phase symptoms and characteristic functional decline. He has no hallucinations, a followable thought process, and 9 years of stable employment — these are attenuated psychotic-like features within a stable lifelong personality pattern.

questions.eli5: He dresses oddly, talks oddly, thinks he can change traffic lights with his mind, and believes the TV is speaking to him — but he has never heard voices and has held the same job for nine years. That mix of odd beliefs plus social fear is schizotypal.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man is referred for evaluation after being placed on a performance plan at the consulting firm where he works. He opened the interview by asking whether the physician trained at 'a real program' and stated that he had specifically requested the department chair. He describes his colleagues as 'competent enough to carry my bags' and reports that he stopped speaking to a longtime friend after that friend received an industry award, calling the selection committee 'clearly corrupt.' He reports fantasies of being recruited to run a national firm and states he expects his current employer will 'realize what they had' after he leaves. When told the physician cannot extend the appointment beyond its scheduled end, he becomes cold and dismissive. He has no history of arrests, deceitfulness, or aggression, and reports stable long-term housing and employment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Narcissistic personality disorder is captured by A FAME GAME: need for admiration, fantasies of unlimited success, arrogance, manipulativeness, envy, grandiosity, association with special or high-status people, a me-first orientation, and lack of empathy. Every one of those appears here — demanding the department chair, denigrating colleagues, cutting off a friend out of envy, fantasies of running a national firm, and cold dismissal when a request for special treatment is refused. Board pearl — the histrionic-versus-narcissistic split is drama and attention-seeking versus grandiosity and superiority; both want to be the center of the room, but for different reasons.  [Learning objectives: LO 041]

wrongExplanations.0: Antisocial personality disorder requires a pervasive disregard for the rights of others with deceitfulness, aggression, irresponsibility, and documented conduct disorder before age 15. The stem explicitly notes no arrests, no deceitfulness, no aggression, and stable housing and employment.
wrongExplanations.1: Borderline personality disorder centers on abandonment fear, unstable relationships and identity, chronic emptiness, and self-harm. His self-image is stably inflated rather than unstable, and no self-harm or identity disturbance is described.
wrongExplanations.3: Histrionic personality disorder involves attention-seeking through theatricality, seductiveness, and shifting shallow emotion with impressionistic speech. He seeks admiration for superiority rather than attention through drama.
wrongExplanations.4: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder centers on rigid perfectionism, excessive devotion to work, inability to delegate, and miserliness. He denigrates colleagues rather than refusing to delegate to them, and no perfectionism or rigidity is described.

questions.eli5: He wants only the most important doctor, looks down on everyone he works with, cannot stand that a friend won an award, and turns cold the moment he does not get special treatment. That is narcissistic personality disorder.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman comes to the office accompanied by her mother, who answers most of the intake questions. The patient states she cannot decide whether to accept a job offer and asks the physician to tell her what to do; when asked her own preference, she says she would rather someone else choose. She has lived with her parents her entire adult life and reports feeling 'panicky and helpless' during the two weeks they traveled without her last year. She remained for 6 years in a relationship in which her partner belittled her publicly, explaining that being alone would have been worse, and began a new relationship 9 days after it ended. She goes to unusual lengths to obtain support, including volunteering for tasks she finds unpleasant so that others will approve of her. She denies fear of criticism as her reason for avoiding decisions, stating instead that she simply does not trust her own judgment. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dependent personality disorder is a pervasive need to be taken care of leading to submissive, clinging behavior and fear of separation — the DARN HURT pattern: difficulty disagreeing, needing advice and reassurance to make decisions, delegating responsibility, going to lengths to obtain nurturance, feeling helpless when alone, unrealistic preoccupation with being left to care for oneself, urgently seeking a new relationship when one ends, and difficulty initiating tasks independently. Board pearl — the Cluster C sibling to rule out is avoidant PD, and the discriminator is the reason for the behavior: avoidant patients hold back because they fear criticism and rejection, whereas dependent patients hand decisions over because they do not trust their own judgment, which is exactly the distinction she draws herself.  [Learning objectives: LO 041]

wrongExplanations.0: Avoidant personality disorder involves social inhibition driven by fear of criticism, rejection, and embarrassment, with feelings of inadequacy. She explicitly denies fear of criticism as her motivation and actively seeks out relationships rather than avoiding them.
wrongExplanations.1: Borderline personality disorder involves frantic efforts to avoid abandonment within a pattern of unstable, intense relationships marked by idealization and devaluation, plus identity disturbance and self-harm. Her relationships are stably submissive rather than turbulent, and no self-harm or splitting is described.
wrongExplanations.2: Histrionic personality disorder centers on attention-seeking, theatricality, seductiveness, and shallow shifting emotions. She is self-effacing and deferential rather than dramatic.
wrongExplanations.3: Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder centers on perfectionism, rigidity, control, and excessive devotion to work. She surrenders control rather than insisting on it.

questions.eli5: She cannot make her own decisions, panics when her parents leave, stayed for years with someone who treated her badly rather than be alone, and found a new partner within days. That is dependent personality disorder.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is brought to the juvenile court clinic for evaluation. Records document that beginning at age 11 he has repeatedly initiated physical fights, set two fires in an abandoned building, killed a neighbor's cat, broken into a garage and stolen tools, and been truant from school more than 60 days in the past year. He shows no remorse, stating that the cat's owner 'should have kept it inside.' He has never had a period of elevated or expansive mood, decreased need for sleep, or grandiosity, and urine toxicology screening is negative. Cognitive testing shows an IQ in the average range, and he has no history of head injury. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: He meets the full behavioral pattern — aggression toward people and animals, destruction of property by fire-setting, deceitfulness and theft, and serious violations of rules — which is conduct disorder. The buried clue is his age. Antisocial personality disorder requires the person to be at least 18 years old AND to have documented evidence of conduct disorder before age 15. He satisfies the childhood-onset half but is only 16, so the adult diagnosis is not yet available to him. Board pearl — this pair is the same behavioral pattern read at two different ages: conduct disorder is the childhood and adolescent version, and it converts to antisocial personality disorder once the person turns 18 if the pattern persists.  [Learning objectives: LO 041, 105]

wrongExplanations.1: Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18, no matter how complete the behavioral picture. He is 16, which is the single detail that blocks this otherwise-tempting answer.
wrongExplanations.2: Oppositional defiant disorder involves an angry and irritable mood, argumentative and defiant behavior toward authority figures, and vindictiveness for at least 6 months — but not the aggression toward people and animals, property destruction, theft, and serious rule violations described here. Those escalate the diagnosis past ODD.
wrongExplanations.3: Intermittent explosive disorder involves recurrent, impulsive aggressive outbursts grossly out of proportion to provocation, without the premeditated deceit, theft, fire-setting, and truancy seen here. His acts are planned and instrumental, not purely explosive.
wrongExplanations.4: ADHD requires inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms present before age 12 across at least two settings. Impulsivity alone does not account for cruelty to animals, fire-setting, burglary, and absence of remorse.

questions.eli5: He fights, sets fires, steals, skips school, and hurt an animal without feeling bad about it. That whole pattern has an adult name, but you have to be eighteen to get it — at sixteen it is called conduct disorder.

questions.stem: Cluster A personality disorders share a familial and genetic association with which of the following?
questions.explanation: The three clusters each carry a distinct genetic neighborhood. Cluster A — paranoid, schizoid, and schizotypal, the odd and eccentric or 'weird' group — overlaps phenomenologically with the negative symptoms of schizophrenia and shows a genetic link to it, with schizotypal having the strongest and most specific association. Cluster B, the dramatic and erratic or 'wild' group, links genetically to mood and substance use disorders. Cluster C, the anxious and fearful or 'worried' group, links to anxiety disorders. Board pearl — this is why schizotypal personality disorder is the personality disorder most often found among the biological relatives of patients with schizophrenia.  [Learning objectives: LO 069]

wrongExplanations.0: Anxiety disorders are the genetic neighborhood of Cluster C — avoidant, dependent, and obsessive-compulsive personality disorders — which share an underlying anxious symptomatology.
wrongExplanations.1: Substance use disorders link to Cluster B, alongside mood disorders, reflecting that group's affective instability and impulsivity.
wrongExplanations.2: Bipolar and related disorders fall under the Cluster B mood-disorder association, not Cluster A.
wrongExplanations.4: Neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and ADHD are not the taught genetic association for any personality disorder cluster.

questions.eli5: The three groups of personality disorders each run in families alongside a different illness. The odd, eccentric group runs with schizophrenia; the dramatic group with mood and drug problems; the anxious group with anxiety disorders.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old nurse is admitted for the fifth time in 2 years for recurrent episodes of severe hypoglycemia. Each admission has been preceded by a witnessed collapse at work. Serum studies during the current episode show glucose 32 mg/dL, insulin 88 microunits/mL, and C-peptide 0.2 ng/mL. Imaging of the pancreas is normal. A housekeeper reports finding vials of insulin and used syringes in the patient's personal bag. She has no diabetes and is not prescribed insulin. She has stable finances, no pending litigation or disability claim, and no legal charges. She asks repeatedly when the next diagnostic procedure will be scheduled, expresses enthusiasm about an upcoming endoscopy, and has told several staff members that she is 'a medical mystery.' Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: B. Factitious disorder imposed on self
F. Factitious disorder imposed on another
questions.explanation: Run the decision tree: is production of the symptom conscious? Yes — she is covertly injecting insulin. Then ask what the goal is. External gain such as money, drugs, or avoiding charges means malingering; the sick role itself, an internal or primary gain, means factitious disorder. She has no financial, legal, or disability incentive, and she actively welcomes procedures and relishes being a medical mystery, which is the sick role. The laboratory pattern seals the mechanism: high insulin with a LOW C-peptide proves the insulin is exogenous, since endogenous secretion would raise both. Board pearl — malingerers avoid invasive procedures because the goal is the payoff, not the process; factitious patients welcome them.  [Learning objectives: LO 014, 031, 039]

wrongExplanations.0: Conversion disorder produces neurologic symptoms — weakness, blindness, non-epileptic seizures — through unconscious mechanisms, with findings internally inconsistent on examination. She is deliberately injecting insulin, which is conscious production of a metabolic, not neurologic, abnormality.
wrongExplanations.2: Illness anxiety disorder is preoccupation with having a serious illness in the setting of minimal or absent somatic symptoms. Her hypoglycemia is objectively real and self-induced; she is manufacturing disease rather than fearing it.
wrongExplanations.3: Malingering requires conscious feigning for an external incentive. The stem explicitly negates every one — stable finances, no litigation, no disability claim, no charges — and her enthusiasm for further procedures is the opposite of malingering behavior.
wrongExplanations.4: Somatic symptom disorder involves excessive thoughts, feelings, and behaviors about genuine somatic symptoms over at least 6 months, with UNCONSCIOUS production. Her symptom production is deliberate.
wrongExplanations.5: Factitious disorder imposed on another is caregiver-induced illness in a child or dependent adult, which constitutes abuse and is a mandatory report. She is inducing illness in herself.

questions.eli5: She is secretly giving herself insulin to make her blood sugar crash. The lab proves the insulin came from a needle, not her body, and she is doing it to be a patient — not for money or to get out of trouble.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because she is unable to walk. She states that yesterday afternoon, about 2 hours after learning that her father had died unexpectedly, both of her legs 'stopped working.' She has no history of trauma, neurologic disease, or psychiatric illness. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F) and vital signs are otherwise within normal limits. On examination she cannot lift either leg against gravity when asked directly, but when the examiner tests hip flexion on the right, strong involuntary extension is felt in the contralateral heel. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric, plantar responses are flexor, sensation is intact to light touch and pinprick in a distribution that does not follow any dermatome, and rectal tone is normal. MRI of the brain and the entire spine shows no abnormality. She discusses her inability to walk in a calm, matter-of-fact manner and appears untroubled by the prospect of permanent paralysis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
choices: B. Factitious disorder imposed on self
questions.explanation: Conversion disorder, also called functional neurological symptom disorder, is an acute sensory or motor deficit that follows a psychological stressor and is internally inconsistent on examination — here the positive Hoover sign, where involuntary contralateral hip extension appears during voluntary hip flexion testing, proving the motor pathway is intact. The non-dermatomal sensory level, normal reflexes, and normal imaging point the same way. Her calm, untroubled affect in the face of dramatic paralysis is la belle indifférence, the classic accompanying sign. Board pearl — production here is UNCONSCIOUS: she genuinely believes she cannot walk, which is what separates conversion from the two conscious deceptions.  [Learning objectives: LO 014, 031, 039]

wrongExplanations.0: Malingering requires conscious feigning for an external incentive such as money, drugs, or avoiding legal consequences. No secondary gain is described, and the symptom arose within hours of a bereavement rather than in pursuit of a payoff.
wrongExplanations.1: Factitious disorder requires intentional falsification of symptoms to assume the sick role. Her deficit is unconsciously produced, and she is not seeking procedures or hospitalization; she was brought in by others.
wrongExplanations.3: Somatic symptom disorder involves excessive thoughts, feelings, and behaviors about somatic symptoms persisting 6 or more months, typically across multiple body systems. Hers is a single dramatic neurologic deficit of one day's duration, and she is notably UNconcerned rather than excessively worried.
wrongExplanations.4: Illness anxiety disorder centers on preoccupation with having a serious illness with minimal or no somatic symptoms present. She has a prominent physical deficit and no preoccupying fear of disease — the opposite pattern on both counts.

questions.eli5: Two hours after hearing her father died, her legs stopped working — but a special test shows the nerves and muscles are fine, and she is oddly calm about it. Her mind, not her spine, produced the paralysis, and she is not faking.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man comes to the office requesting a repeat neurologic evaluation. For the past 3 years he has been convinced that he has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. He has undergone four full neurologic workups, including two electromyography studies and MRI of the brain and cervical spine, all normal, and has seen three different neurologists. His only physical complaint is occasional twitching of the calf muscles, which he acknowledges is intermittent and painless. He inspects his tongue and calves in the mirror daily for atrophy, times how long he can hold a grip, and reads ALS forums for several hours each week. Reassurance from a physician relieves him for about 3 days, after which the worry returns in full. He works full-time and reports no depressed mood, no obsessive thoughts he regards as senseless, and no rituals performed to neutralize anxiety. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The discriminator between the two somatoform siblings is which side dominates: real physical complaints, or the fear about them. In somatic symptom disorder the somatic complaints are prominent and multi-system; in illness anxiety disorder the preoccupation with HAVING a specific serious illness dominates while somatic symptoms are minimal or absent. His only physical symptom is occasional painless twitching — trivial — while three years of checking, forum-reading, and doctor-shopping consume his life, and reassurance holds for only days. Board pearl — care-seeking behavior with repeated workups is characteristic, and the persistence despite four normal evaluations is the diagnostic feature rather than evidence that something was missed.  [Learning objectives: LO 014, 039]

wrongExplanations.0: Body dysmorphic disorder is preoccupation with a perceived defect in physical appearance that is minor or unobservable to others, occupying an hour or more daily. His preoccupation is with having a disease, not with how he looks.
wrongExplanations.1: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive worry across multiple everyday domains for more than 6 months with associated symptoms such as restlessness, fatigue, and muscle tension. His worry is confined to a single theme.
wrongExplanations.2: OCD requires obsessions the patient recognizes as intrusive and unwanted, typically paired with compulsions performed to neutralize anxiety. He explicitly reports no thoughts he regards as senseless and no neutralizing rituals; his checking is illness-focused reassurance-seeking rather than a compulsion.
wrongExplanations.4: Somatic symptom disorder requires prominent, distressing somatic symptoms. His single symptom is occasional painless twitching, which is minimal — the fear, not the symptom, is the whole clinical picture.
wrongExplanations.5: Malingering requires conscious feigning for external gain. He works full-time, seeks no compensation or accommodation, and is genuinely distressed rather than deceptive.

questions.eli5: He barely has any symptoms — just some muscle twitching — but he has spent three years and four normal test batteries convinced he has a fatal nerve disease. When the fear is huge and the symptoms are tiny, that is illness anxiety disorder.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes to the office because of recurrent gaps in her memory. She describes finding unfamiliar clothing in her closet and receiving text messages she has no recollection of sending, and she recently 'came to' in a grocery store 20 miles from home with no memory of driving there. Her husband reports that on several occasions she has spoken in a noticeably higher, childlike voice, referred to herself as 'Katie,' and afterward had no recollection of the conversation. She discloses a history of severe, repeated physical and sexual abuse by a relative between ages 4 and 11. She denies auditory or visual hallucinations and denies fixed false beliefs. Urine toxicology screening is negative, and MRI of the brain and electroencephalography are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dissociative identity disorder requires two or more distinct personality states plus recurrent gaps in recall of everyday events, personal information, or traumatic events. Both halves are present: a distinct state with its own voice and name, and amnesia for the periods when it is present, with evidence of unremembered actions such as purchased clothing and sent texts. Etiologically it is attributed to severe early childhood trauma — repetitive physical, sexual, or emotional abuse — with dissociation acting as a protective mechanism that lets the developing mind compartmentalize unbearable experience. Board pearl — a live debate holds that DID may represent severe chronic PTSD with dissociative features rather than a distinct entity, which is worth knowing as nuance rather than as an answer.  [Learning objectives: LO 030, 078]

wrongExplanations.1: Dissociative amnesia is memory loss alone, without alternate identity states. The distinguishing feature here is that her husband witnesses a distinct state with a different voice and a different name — memory gaps by themselves would not capture that.
wrongExplanations.2: Depersonalization/derealization disorder involves feeling detached from oneself or one's surroundings with reality testing fully intact. It does not include amnesia for events or alternate identity states.
wrongExplanations.3: Schizophrenia requires active-phase psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized speech for a significant portion of at least 6 months. She explicitly denies hallucinations and fixed false beliefs, and identity states are not psychosis.
wrongExplanations.4: Borderline personality disorder can include transient stress-related dissociative symptoms and micropsychotic episodes, but it is defined by unstable relationships, identity disturbance, impulsivity, and abandonment fear — none of which is described. Discrete alternate identity states with amnesia go beyond borderline's transient dissociation.

questions.eli5: She loses chunks of time, finds clothes she never bought, and her husband has seen her speak in a child's voice using a different name. That, on top of severe abuse as a young child, is dissociative identity disorder.

questions.stem: Which of the following features best distinguishes depersonalization/derealization disorder from a primary psychotic disorder?
choices: A. The presence of auditory hallucinations
B. Loss of memory for personal identity
C. The presence of two or more distinct identity states
D. Onset after 40 years of age
questions.explanation: In depersonalization/derealization disorder the patient feels detached from their own body, thoughts, or surroundings — but knows the experience is not literally true, saying things like 'it feels as though I am watching myself from outside my body, but I know I am not.' That intact reality testing is the boundary between the dissociative spectrum and psychosis, where the patient's beliefs and perceptions are held as real. Board pearl — keep the terms straight: depersonalization refers to detachment from the SELF, derealization to detachment from the ENVIRONMENT, and both commonly occur during panic attacks, which is where students most often encounter them.  [Learning objectives: LO 078]

wrongExplanations.0: Auditory hallucinations are a psychotic symptom and are not a feature of depersonalization/derealization disorder at all, so their presence would point away from the dissociative diagnosis rather than distinguish it.
wrongExplanations.1: Loss of memory for personal identity characterizes dissociative amnesia, particularly with the fugue specifier. Depersonalization/derealization does not involve amnesia.
wrongExplanations.2: Two or more distinct identity states is the defining criterion of dissociative identity disorder, a different diagnosis within the same chapter.
wrongExplanations.3: Age of onset does not distinguish these conditions. Depersonalization/derealization typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood, which does not separate it from a first psychotic episode either.

questions.eli5: Someone with this condition feels unreal or outside their body, but they know that feeling is not actually true. Knowing it is not real is exactly what makes it different from psychosis.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man is seen for couples therapy focused on communication difficulties. During an individual session he discloses that since adolescence he has experienced recurrent, intense sexual arousal in association with a specific inanimate object. His wife has been aware of this for the entire 14 years of their marriage, participates willingly, and describes it as an unremarkable part of their relationship. He reports no distress about the interest itself, states it has never interfered with his work or social functioning, and has never involved anyone who did not consent. He has no other psychiatric history, and his presenting concern is entirely about how he and his wife argue about finances. Which of the following most accurately characterizes his sexual interest?
choices: B. A paraphilia that does not meet criteria for a paraphilic disorder
questions.explanation: The distinction that matters is paraphilia versus paraphilic DISORDER. A paraphilia is an atypical sexual interest, ascertained by self-report or behavior, and it is not by itself a diagnosis. It rises to a paraphilic disorder only if it causes the person distress or functional impairment, or causes harm to others. He reports no distress, no impairment, and a consenting partner — so no diagnosis applies. Board pearl — voyeuristic, exhibitionistic, and frotteuristic disorders, along with any sexual contact with a child, inherently involve a non-consenting party and therefore meet the harm criterion by definition, which is why those are always disorders when acted upon.  [Learning objectives: LO 033, 034]

wrongExplanations.0: Fetishistic disorder would require the interest to cause clinically significant distress or impairment in functioning. His marriage is intact, his wife participates willingly, and his work and social life are unaffected — the diagnostic threshold is simply not crossed.
wrongExplanations.2: The other specified category is used for a paraphilia that causes distress or impairment but does not fit one of the eight named disorders, such as asphyxiophilia. His interest fits a named category and, more importantly, causes no distress or impairment.
wrongExplanations.3: Voyeuristic disorder involves arousal from observing an unsuspecting person who is undressing or engaged in sexual activity, which inherently involves a non-consenting party. His interest is in an inanimate object with a consenting spouse.
wrongExplanations.4: Sexual masochism disorder involves arousal from being humiliated, beaten, bound, or made to suffer. That is not what is described, and the distress or impairment criterion would still be unmet.
wrongExplanations.5: Transvestic disorder involves arousal from cross-dressing. The interest described is in an inanimate object rather than in wearing clothing of another gender, and again no distress, impairment, or harm is present.

questions.eli5: Having an unusual sexual interest is not the same as having a disorder. It only becomes a diagnosis if it upsets the person, wrecks their life, or hurts somebody who did not agree — and none of those is true here.
